lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Road Rehabilitation and Maintenance Project (P071985), SDR 33.5 million (US$50 million equivalent) approved 9 March 2004, with a first additional financing of SDR 16.8 million (US$25 million) and a second of SDR 9.9 million (US$15 million); the completion report's cover gives the credit numbers as IDA-38660, IDA-38661 and IDPA-48210. SDR 59.98 million was disbursed. The project closed on 30 June 2014, seven years after its first closing date. The credit paid for the rehabilitation of 39 km of the Chingola-Kasumbalesa road and for its engineering supervision. The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the implementing agencies' performance Moderately Unsatisfactory (27 April 2015); the Independent Evaluation Group rates the outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance all Moderately Unsatisfactory.

companies.name: Road Development Agency
companies.role: Implementing agency for the road works and the channel through which the compensation receipts were to be passed to the lender
companies.desc: Zambian state road agency, set up in 2005 under this project together with the National Road Fund Agency and the Road Transport and Safety Agency, responsible for the trunk road network.

kasumbalesa-market-traders-moved.community: In December 2005 traders were moved from the north-eastern side of the Chingola-Kasumbalesa road to the western side, to clear space for trucks waiting to be cleared by immigration at the border. The Environmental Management Unit of the Roads Department, which was responsible for applying the lender's resettlement rules, was told only after the move had happened. The abbreviated resettlement plan written afterwards, in May 2006, states that "because of lack of information and sensitization, the provisions outlined in the Resettlement Policy Framework completed during project preparation have not been followed", and that the plan was written to correct that. The plan lists 67 numbered traders by name and national registration number, some names appearing more than once, and puts the number of people at roughly 65: 23 restaurants, 20 grocery stalls, 21 sellers of vegetables, fruit and other goods, one carpentry business and two pay phones. The sums set were 2,590,000 kwacha for each restaurant, 1,390,000 for each grocery, 400,000 for each market seller, 250,000 for the carpentry and 8,000,000 for each pay phone, 113,410,000 kwacha in all. The costs counted were taking down and rebuilding structures, buying materials, business lost during the move, and transport of materials from Chililabombwe 20 km away. The plan says the host community was the same community, because the move was within the same area, and that the facilities used before the move still served the people who were resettled. Elsewhere on the same project, a resettlement plan costing US$3.5 million was prepared and carried out for 333 people in 57 households affected by the construction of Mufuchani Bridge, and four people whose small business stood in the way of Chiawa Bridge had it moved. The completion report says the government's share of the money was not paid on schedule, which caused "major delays in implementing the Resettlement Action Plan" and in turn hit the project timetable and costs.
kasumbalesa-market-traders-moved.displaced_label: people (traders) moved, from the abbreviated resettlement plan for the Kasumbalesa border post, May 2006
kasumbalesa-market-traders-moved.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 67 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The resettlement plan's table has 67 numbered entries, with some names repeating, and the plan's own text puts the number of people at roughly 65.
kasumbalesa-market-traders-moved.outcome: The plan set out that the contractor would pay each trader in front of a council officer and an officer of the Environmental Management Unit, that each would sign a receipt, and that the signed receipts would go to the Resident Engineer as part of the contractor's monthly claim and on to the Road Development Agency, the National Road Fund Agency and the World Bank. Neither the completion report nor the Evaluation Group's review of it says whether the money was paid. The completion report's table of safeguard documents records the abbreviated plan as disclosed in July 2006. The road was rehabilitated; the Evaluation Group's review says that at closing several sections, among them Chingola-Kasumbalesa, were in poor condition and in further need of repair.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Second Phase of the Roads and Bridges Management and Maintenance Program (P083325), Credit 4308-MZ of SDR 66.1 million (US$100 million equivalent) approved 23 May 2007, with Credit 4892-MZ of SDR 26.3 million (US$41 million), Grant H904-MZ of SDR 23.7 million (US$36.25 million), Credit 5346-MZ of SDR 2.1 million (US$3.15 million) and Credit 5602-MZ of SDR 52.3 million (US$73.6 million). jardim-benfica-road-resettlement.community: The 7 km Jardim-Benfica section of the N1 north of Maputo was widened to a four-lane divided carriageway 13.6 metres wide. The appraisal document says the environmental assessment found that housing, along with shops, kiosks and fences, would be hit along the section, and that a resettlement plan was written to cover "displacement of individuals and structures and their resettlement", with provision for repositioning structures within the existing area where possible, for paying compensation before property was removed, and for employing affected people. The completion report records that there was engagement with affected people throughout, "especially where the PAPs along the Jardim-Benfica Road who were displaced by the road works and were consequently relocated to a new settlement". Neither the completion report nor the Evaluation Group's review of it gives a number for those people, names the new settlement, or says what they were paid. The same paragraph of the report says the project was generally carried out in line with the safeguard frameworks and plans, that the road administration's environmental and social unit performed strongly, and that an external audit of the resettlement plan was rated satisfactory. For the emergency works added to the project later, the report says no land acquisition was necessary and there was no loss of other assets or crops.
jardim-benfica-road-resettlement.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 85 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No World Bank document opened for this project counts the people relocated from the Jardim-Benfica road.
jardim-benfica-road-resettlement.outcome: The section was finished and the completion report says the flow of traffic improved because the road now has enough capacity for it. The project ran for eleven and a half years. No document opened records what happened to the people after they were moved.

kampala-records-centre-households-moved.title: Seven Households Moved for a Records Centre That Never Opened
kampala-records-centre-households-moved.place: Plot 8-10 Lourdel Road, Upper Kitante, Kampala, Uganda
kampala-records-centre-households-moved.point: OpenStreetMap node for Lourdel Road in Kitante, Kampala. The plot number given in the resettlement plan was not separately located.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Public Service Performance Enhancement Project (P050440), Credit IDA-41990 of SDR 14.0 million (US$23 million equivalent) approved 20 June 2006, effective 19 November 2008, closed 30 June 2014 after an extension of two and a half years. Sub-component 1.4 financed the construction of the National Records Centre and Archives. The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory, the risk to the development outcome Substantial, Bank performance Moderately Unsatisfactory and borrower performance Unsatisfactory (26 February 2015).

companies.name: Ministry of Public Service
companies.role: Chose the site, wrote and carried out the resettlement plan and built the centre
companies.desc: The Ugandan ministry responsible for public service management, pay and records; its Project Coordination Unit ran this project and sat on the compensation committee.

kampala-records-centre-households-moved.community: Seven households, 56 people in all, lived in government houses on the plot picked for the National Records Centre and Archives. The abbreviated resettlement plan of October 2006 names each head of household and gives their job: a town clerk at Kampala City Council, an office attendant, an assistant commissioner, a driver, a principal nursing officer at Mulago Hospital and others, most of them government employees. The census, dated 3 November 2005, records households of between four and seventeen people living in one- to three-bedroom houses, several of them growing maize, cassava, beans, bananas, mangoes, pawpaw and sugar cane in their yards. Stays ran from one year to sixteen years. Some households had no allocation letter; one man had been told verbally that he could occupy the house. The plan says these were the last batch of government pool houses, that the heads of household knew the policy had changed and that the houses were due for demolition, and that they stayed on until the land was wanted. The plan sets the entitlement at six months' rent, one year's value of crops and the full cost of transport: 1,800,000 Uganda shillings for each household, 100,000 each for moving, and 100,000 more for the five households with crops, 13,800,000 shillings in all. Finding somewhere else to rent was left to the households themselves. The plan records that the households had no fixed structures or assets that could be lost, that the two grandchildren in one household had never been to school, and that one man had no identity card, had tried once to get one and lacked witnesses. The completion report says there were people living at the site who had to be relocated, and that the ministry held meetings with them to carry out the plan's recommendations. The Evaluation Group's review says the same: people living on the site had to be relocated. Neither document counts the people actually moved.
kampala-records-centre-households-moved.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 56 for this project. That is the number of people the October 2006 resettlement plan counted living on the site before the move, not a count of people a World Bank document records as moved.
kampala-records-centre-households-moved.outcome: The building was finished before the project closed on 30 June 2014. It was never furnished and never brought into use. The completion report records that no records had been transferred to it, that the share of semi-active records moved there stood at zero against a target of 60 per cent, and that it is questionable whether the centre will help clear the congestion in government registries. The report also says government continues to bear the cost of an inefficient records system and that many national records continue to be lost and degraded.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Urban Infrastructure and City Management Project (P060005), Grant IDA-H1880 of SDR 13.9 million (US$20 million equivalent) approved 10 November 2005, effective 2 June 2006, closed 31 December 2009 after a nine-month extension. One sub-component paid for the resettlement action plans and for any unexpected resettlement arising from the infrastructure sub-projects. The completion report rates the outcome Highly Satisfactory (24 June 2010); the Evaluation Group's field assessment, based on a January 2018 visit, lowers that to Satisfactory and lowers borrower performance from Highly Satisfactory to Satisfactory (20 December 2018).

companies.name: Ministry of Infrastructure (MININFRA)

companies.desc: The Rwandan ministry responsible for transport, energy, water and public works; it appointed the resettlement committee for this project.

kigali-huye-musanze-urban-works-compensa.community: The project paved and drained urban roads in Kigali and in the secondary cities of Huye and Musanze. The completion report says the resettlement plans were completed and that "a total of 866 persons were compensated in accordance with the Resettlement Action Plans". The Evaluation Group's field assessment repeats the figure. Neither document says what the 866 lost or how many of them moved. The abbreviated resettlement plan of October 2006, for the first phase of road works in Kigali and Huye, counts 29 affected households, says the works needed the demolition of the terraces of buildings standing in the road reserve, mostly small shops, and says 17 households on the Kabeza-Rubirizi-Isae stretch would not be compensated and would have to move the live hedges and fences standing in the reserve themselves. The report says the use of the resettlement framework caused delays at first because the approach was new in Rwanda and because technical designs had to be changed to reduce the social impact. The Evaluation Group adds that relocation of affected people was one reason the land development pilot ran late. That pilot laid out 33 hectares of serviced land at Akumunigo in Kigali, meant to be divided into plots for low-income households who could be resettled under the project. The Group visited in January 2018 and found the land idle: it was serviced in 2009, the plots have never been handed out, and a plan to develop the area with a private partner fell through when one partner ran into financial trouble.
kigali-huye-musanze-urban-works-compensa.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 42 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The World Bank's completion report counts 866 people compensated under the project's resettlement plans; it does not say how many were moved.
kigali-huye-musanze-urban-works-compensa.outcome: The serviced land at Akumunigo, now called Rugarama, was still unused at the Evaluation Group's visit in January 2018, nine years after it was laid out; the Group calls it inefficient use of project resources and gives it as one reason for lowering the outcome rating. The completion report records that the government wrote the project's resettlement approach into its own compensation and land laws, which the report gives as an indirect result of the lender's safeguard requirements.

kamuzu-barrage-liwonde-businesses.title: Businesses and Fishermen Displaced at the Kamuzu Barrage
kamuzu-barrage-liwonde-businesses.point: OpenStreetMap node for Liwonde town. The barrage stands on the Shire River at Liwonde; its exact point was not separately located.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Shire River Basin Management Program Phase I (P117617), Credit IDA-51250 of SDR 60.6 million (US$93.75 million equivalent) and Grant IDA-H7750 of SDR 20.2 million (US$31.25 million), approved 14 June 2012, effective 7 September 2012, closed 31 January 2019; US$121.88 million of the US$142.88 million was disbursed. The largest investment was the upgrading of the Kamuzu Barrage. The completion report rates the outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation Substantial (3 June 2019).

lenders.name: Global Environment Facility and Least Developed Countries Fund
lenders.role: Grant TF-12920 of US$5.078 million from the GEF Trust Fund and grant TF-12921 of US$1.5 million from the Least Developed Countries Fund, filed under P127866, both fully disbursed

companies.name: Ministry of Agriculture, Irrigation and Water Development
companies.role: Carried out the project through its project management unit, which ran the resettlement plan with district authorities and contractors
companies.desc: The Malawian ministry then responsible for water resources; the project also set up the Shire River Basin Agency, and the National Water Resources Authority began work at the end of the project.

kamuzu-barrage-liwonde-businesses.community: The project rebuilt the Kamuzu Barrage on the Shire River at Liwonde. The completion report says the project's sub-projects did not entail physical relocation, and then records "economic displacement of 22 individual PAPs, 4 institutions (ESCOM, Maritime Police Office, Liwonde Town Council and Liwonde National Park) and 32 Fishermen at both the barrage and SRBA building". The resettlement plan of February 2014 names the people and lists what each stood to lose. One owner faced the complete closure of a camp business on the river, with a boat safari, a bar, restaurants, five guest rooms and twenty campsites. Another faced the replacement of a reception building, a bar, a house, a gate house and an old restaurant, and the loss of business income during construction. A third stood to lose the use of six shops and a dwelling house while the work went on. Eight men are listed each losing a meat-selling business. A bicycle shed, a chip shed and a meat-roasting shed are each listed. Liwonde Town Assembly was to lose the income from six business shelters for three years, and two others the use of bare land, 0.25 and 0.35 hectares, for the three years of construction. The plan records that all of them said they were willing to give up their land provided they were properly compensated, and that they pressed to know when work would start so they could reposition themselves; the valuation team could not tell them. The project's flood-protection structures used voluntary land donation rather than purchase. A grievance system was set up and used, but the completion report says it was "gauged as partially non-inclusive to all PAPs because larger business owners did not use it", and that by project closure one grievance was still unresolved and in the courts. The appraisal document also records that the barrage would lower dry-season water levels upstream in Liwonde National Park, reducing sandbars and floodplain grassland, and that the project area included restrictions on access to grazing in protected catchments.
kamuzu-barrage-liwonde-businesses.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 26 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people. The World Bank's completion report says the project's sub-projects did not entail physical relocation, and counts 22 individual people, four institutions and 32 fishermen economically displaced at the barrage and the Shire River Basin Agency building.
kamuzu-barrage-liwonde-businesses.killed_note: The completion report's economic annex gives 106 people killed in Malawi's 2015 floods and 60 in the 2019 floods. Those are national flood tolls, used to value the damage the project's flood works were meant to avoid; they are not deaths caused by the works.
kamuzu-barrage-liwonde-businesses.outcome: The barrage was finished and the project closed on 31 January 2019 with an outcome rating of Satisfactory. One grievance was still in the courts at closing and no document opened says how it ended. In January 2026 the Malawi Freedom Network reported that lodge owners on the Lake Malawi shore in Mangochi and Salima had sued the National Water Resources Authority and the state generator EGENCO, accusing them of negligence in managing the barrage at Liwonde and saying that this caused flooding along the lake shore. That claim concerns the running of the barrage after the project closed, and it is an allegation in a case that has not been decided.

mafinga-igawa-road-deaths-displacement.title: Deaths and Unapproved Displacement on the Mafinga-Igawa Road
mafinga-igawa-road-deaths-displacement.place: Mafinga-Igawa road, Iringa and Mbeya regions, Tanzania
mafinga-igawa-road-deaths-displacement.point: OpenStreetMap node for Mafinga town in Iringa Region, at one end of the rehabilitated road section. The border post works were at the Songwe/Kasumulu crossing with Malawi, about 400 km further south.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Southern Africa Trade and Transport Facilitation Project, first phase (P120370), Credit IDA-52480 of SDR 138.7 million (US$210 million equivalent) to Tanzania and Grant IDA-H8440 of SDR 2.0 million (US$3 million) to the Dar es Salaam Corridor Committee, approved 21 May 2013, effective 26 November 2013, closed 31 December 2020 after two extensions; US$175.4 million disbursed. The project financed the rehabilitation of the corridor from Igawa to the Zambian border at Tunduma, a one-stop border post at Songwe/Kasumulu and improvements at eight accident black spots. The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory and records a safeguards rating of Moderately Unsatisfactory at closing (28 January 2022). The Evaluation Group rates the quality of supervision Moderately Unsatisfactory and says it is not clear how the Bank addressed the issue of fatalities related to contractors.

companies.name: Tanzania National Roads Agency (TANROADS)
companies.role: Implementing agency for the road works, the border post and the black spot works; began work at one black spot, including displacing people, without preparing the safeguard documents
companies.desc: An executive agency under Tanzania's works ministry that manages and maintains the national trunk and regional road network through regional offices.

mafinga-igawa-road-deaths-displacement.community: Twenty-four people died along the Mafinga-Igawa road while it was being rehabilitated. The completion report counts 104 accidents on the project road during construction, 13 of them fatal, and says that of the 24 deaths "two were attributed to the contractors' employees or involved contractors' employees and/or equipment, with the rest due to road crashes". The report puts the rate at 0.06 deaths per kilometre per year, half the Tanzanian average of 0.11 for trunk roads at the time, which it links to the slower speeds through the works, and then calls that rate "undoubtedly shocking". A road safety audit was carried out and its findings went into the road design. The borrower's comments, printed in the same report, dispute the Bank's account: they give the number as 23, say that calling it a large number "is not evidenced", point out that the report itself records the rate as below the national average, and say there is no evidence for the implied conclusion that the contractors' handling of traffic was insufficient for the traffic on the corridor. On land, the report says resettlement plans were prepared and carried out satisfactorily for most of the works, but that problems remained at closing in two places. At the one-stop border post, "compensation and demolition of property required by the implementation occurred prior to clearance of the RAP". At one of the black spot sites, "works began, including displacement without preparation of safeguards instruments by TANROADS and approval by the WB". The Bank says it kept monitoring after the project closed to ensure its resettlement policy was met and the affected people properly compensated, and that it will do so until all the resettlement issues are addressed. Other safeguard failures the report and the review record are a contractor dumping debris in wetlands and blocking water flow, and diversion roads built for the works left unattended, with erosion then affecting more than 20 km along the corridor.
mafinga-igawa-road-deaths-displacement.killed_note: The completion report counts 24 deaths along the Mafinga-Igawa road during construction, from 104 accidents of which 13 were fatal. Two are counted here because the report ties them to the contractors: they were "attributed to the contractors' employees or involved contractors' employees and/or equipment". The other 22 the report puts down to road crashes and they are not counted. The borrower's comments in the same report give the total as 23.
mafinga-igawa-road-deaths-displacement.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 17 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people. No World Bank document opened for this project counts the people displaced at the border post or at the black spot.
mafinga-igawa-road-deaths-displacement.outcome: The project closed on 31 December 2020 with the border post and the inspection station at Vigwaza still unfinished, to be completed with government money. The time for trucks to cross from Songwe into Malawi rose from 24 hours at appraisal to 72 hours at closing, which the report puts down to the construction still under way and to Covid-19 controls. The resettlement and compensation problems at the border post and at the black spot were unresolved when the project closed, and the project's safeguards rating at closing was Moderately Unsatisfactory.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Zanzibar Urban Services Project (P111155), Credit IDA-48610 of US$38 million approved 24 February 2011 and Credit IDA-58430 of US$55 million as additional financing in June 2016, SDR 63.9 million in all; US$87.57 million disbursed; closed 31 May 2021, five years after its first closing date. The completion report rates the outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation Substantial (23 November 2021); the Evaluation Group records that the overall safeguards compliance rating went to unsatisfactory in March 2013 and stayed in the negative range.

companies.role: Ran the works and the resettlement plans; took statements after each fatal accident and agreed corrective measures with the lender
companies.desc: A unit inside Zanzibar's finance ministry set up to run this project; the completion report says it had no authority over the other ministries and agencies involved.

companies.name: Zanzibar Municipal Council
companies.role: Operated the waste dump site, demolished and compensated one house to open a route for collection vehicles, and began open dumping of waste in Ng'ambo settlements after the dump site closed
companies.desc: The municipal authority for Zanzibar Town, responsible for waste collection in the urban area.

zanzibar-drainage-deaths-compensation.community: Five people died in three accidents on the drainage works between 2015 and 2020. The completion report says the project "encountered weaknesses on the implementation of health and safety issues which led to three severe accidents and five fatalities". A trespasser who broke into a drainage work site through a gap in the fence fell and drowned on 3 April 2016. Two workers died when the soil collapsed at a deep cut on 8 November 2019. Two passengers on a motorcycle died when it crashed into a dump truck working near the Mwanakwerekwe pond on 22 March 2020. After each accident the project team took statements from contractors, workers, consultants and other witnesses, reported to the lender, and agreed corrective measures; the report says site safety and health management improved after those measures. On land and money, the drainage designs were revised during the project and the number of people affected and the cost came out far above the plan; the government could not pay and no land was available for land-for-land swaps, so the credit paid instead. The report says 605 people were compensated for the drainage and solid waste works, "albeit with some delays". A further 167 people in the buffer zone of the Kibele landfill faced delays and incomplete payment because the government budget ran short; after the lender released another US$550,000, all but three had been paid by 1 April 2021. A footnote records that those three could not be reached through radio, newspapers, village leaders "and so on", and that after the loan account closed at the end of September 2021 the government is obliged to pay them if they come forward to claim. The resettlement plan of December 2018 for drainage system C counted 194 affected households and 162 structures, 30 of them to be taken completely: 141 residential structures, of which 30 would be taken entirely and 111 would lose a wall, a verandah, a foundation, a room, a toilet, an outside kitchen or a septic tank; 12 businesses to be closed and moved, among them six at Sogea and shops at Shaurimoyo, Jitimai and Magogoni; and shelters used by widows, disabled people and people with long illnesses who the plan says would need help to move. The November 2017 plan for the Kibele landfill counted 60 individual landholders, of whom 13 living in occupied dwellings, with 57 household members, were to be moved out of the project area. The municipal council demolished one house, with compensation, to open a route for collection vehicles into a dense settlement where people had been throwing their rubbish into the drain. The Evaluation Group also records that the existing dump site, which the project had assumed would last five years, was closed during the project by community opposition unconnected to the project, after which the council "began open dumping of waste in Ng'ambo settlements causing an environmental and public health crisis".
zanzibar-drainage-deaths-compensation.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 14 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people. The World Bank's completion report counts 605 people compensated for the drainage and waste works and 167 more in the Kibele landfill buffer zone. It does not count the people moved. The counts of 194 households, 162 structures and 13 dwellings come from the project's resettlement plans and are what was planned.
zanzibar-drainage-deaths-compensation.killed_note: The five deaths are counted because the completion report gives a cause for each that ties it to the works: a gap in the fence at a drainage site, a soil collapse at a deep cut, and a dump truck working near the Mwanakwerekwe pond. The report attributes the three accidents to weaknesses in carrying out health and safety measures. The Evaluation Group's review repeats all three accounts.
zanzibar-drainage-deaths-compensation.outcome: The project closed on 31 May 2021 with an outcome rating of Satisfactory. Three people in the Kibele landfill buffer zone had still not been paid when the loan account closed at the end of September 2021, and the government was notified of its obligation to pay them in future. The completion report says overall safeguards management, occupational health and site safety improved after the accidents.

The loan closed on 30 June 2014 and the guarantee on 9 September 2015. The completion report rates the outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance all Unsatisfactory and the risk to the development outcome High (6 October 2016); the Evaluation Group agrees with all four ratings.

lenders.name: African Development Bank, Industrial and Commercial Bank of China and Sinosure
lenders.role: Co-financiers and partners named in the completion report's data sheet

companies.name: Botswana Power Corporation (BPC)
companies.role: State utility that built and runs the plant, handled the resettlement and the compensation on the transmission corridors, and was found by the lender's mission to be weak in enforcing safety standards
companies.desc: Botswana's state-owned electricity utility, which generates, transmits and distributes power; it set up the project management unit for this project.

companies.name: China National Electronic Equipment Corporation (CNEEC)

morupule-b-family-moved-fatal-accidents.community: One family lived on the footprint of the power station: a woman of 97, her daughter, the daughter's husband and their granddaughter, with a grandson who lived in Palapye and visited. Their home was two small huts built mainly of scrap and found materials, a store and a fence, on about 2,000 square metres of yard and field. They had three donkeys and a donkey cart, which they used to fetch water from outside, and they lived on firewood, mopane worms and fruit they collected and sold in Palapye and on crops they grew for themselves. The abbreviated resettlement plan of May 2009 records that they did not plant their usual food crops that year because they knew they would be moved, and that they were to be compensated for that lost harvest. Two plots were cleared for them about 5 to 6 km from Palapye, each to get a house of 3.4 by 10 metres and a pit latrine; while that was built the family was housed in tents on the plots, and the plan says they were to be moved on 25 May 2009. The family asked to stay about the same distance from Palapye so they could keep travelling there daily and keep their way of living. The plan also records that neither grandchild had ever been to school, and that the husband had no identity card, had tried once to get one and lacked the witnesses he needed. On the transmission line corridors, the Evaluation Group records that compensation was paid to informal settlers, that one house had to be demolished with its owner moved to a nearby town, that the works affected about 130 households, and that two landowners complained about the compensation terms and about a borehole being moved, both complaints being settled. Five fatal accidents happened at the plant: in February 2011, August 2011, September 2012, December 2013 and March 2015. All but the December 2013 accident were falls from height; that one the report puts down to poor coordination of repairs, and the March 2015 one was a fall from height during boiler repair work. The completion report says safety remained a serious concern throughout the project, with weaknesses in enforcing safety standards and procedures, a lax safety environment, and weak control of who entered and left the site for much of the construction. An action plan was agreed after the first accident and widened after the second, when the lender's October 2011 mission "confirmed a serious lack of safety enforcement by the EPC contractor". Only after the third accident did the utility suspend work at height, tighten site security and hire both a safety supervision firm and a separate scaffolding contractor; police officers were deployed to enforce site security. The environment department and the waste management department made frequent site visits and fines were levied on the utility and the contractor for breaches over hygiene, waste disposal, sewage ponds, oil and acid storage and insufficient dust suppression. Noise in parts of the plant exceeded both the contract requirements and industry standards.
morupule-b-family-moved-fatal-accidents.displaced_label: people - the family of four resident on the power station footprint, from the abbreviated resettlement plan of May 2009
morupule-b-family-moved-fatal-accidents.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 5 for this project. The resettlement plan says "one family of four is resident" on the power station footprint, and its census table lists five family members, the fifth living in Palapye with friends and visiting. The Evaluation Group's review says the resettlement of the family "had been completed satisfactorily, as reported". One further household was moved from a transmission line corridor after its house was demolished.
morupule-b-family-moved-fatal-accidents.suppression: Mmegi reported on 8 January 2016 that thirty workers employed by NEPEC 11, a subcontractor at the plant, said they had been retrenched after stopping work in December over safety, pay and their contracts. They said they worked near high-voltage electricity, with dust and chemicals, and at height, without protective equipment, a risk allowance or medical checks, and that they believed they were singled out for raising their rights. The company's translator and secretariat, Jia Zhu, denied the dismissals had anything to do with the stoppage, said most of the work at the plant was finished so fewer workers were needed, and said the company had never given the workers medical examinations, not even when it hired them. The Palapye labour office had not settled the matter and set a hearing for 29 February 2016.
morupule-b-family-moved-fatal-accidents.killed_note: The World Bank's completion report records five fatal accidents at the Morupule B construction site, in February 2011, August 2011, September 2012, December 2013 and March 2015, and gives a cause for each: falls from height in all but the December 2013 accident, which it puts down to poor coordination of repairs. The report does not state a number of people killed; five is the number of fatal accidents it records. Global Energy Monitor's entry on the plant, citing Mmegi of 30 July 2015, says at least two Chinese workers died during construction and that some Botswana workers were injured through lax observation of safety principles.
morupule-b-family-moved-fatal-accidents.outcome: The plant was built but has run far below what was expected: it was meant to work at an annual capacity factor of about 80 per cent and has not. The completion report rates the project Unsatisfactory on outcome, on Bank performance and on borrower performance, and the risk to the development outcome High, and the Evaluation Group agrees. Emissions from the stacks were not measured reliably because the instruments malfunctioned or were not calibrated, and the report says sulphur oxide emissions were likely to have breached the standards whenever the limestone injection system broke down. Ambient air quality data only became available in August 2015, from a single monitoring station moved over from the older Morupule A plant.

burundi-fibre-backbone-unpaid-compensati.place: Burundi's national fibre backbone, Bujumbura, Burundi

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Regional Communications Infrastructure Project, first phase (P094103), approved 29 March 2007, closed 31 December 2016 after nine restructurings. Burundi's share was Grant H283-BI, estimated at US$20.10 million at appraisal, with US$20.60 million disbursed, inside a three-country operation covering Burundi, Kenya and Madagascar whose grant estimate rose from US$164.5 million to US$249.6 million. The three countries contributed nothing of the US$37.40 million expected of them. The Evaluation Group rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory.

companies.name: Burundi Backbone System (BBS)
companies.role: The company that built and ran the national fibre network under the project; the state revoked its public-private status and nationalised it in January 2017
companies.desc: A Burundian company set up under this project with private sector participation to build and operate the national fibre backbone and sell capacity to operators.

burundi-fibre-backbone-unpaid-compensati.community: The project laid 1,254 km of fibre optic cable across Burundi, reaching 34 communes, and linked 58 government institutions and 14 universities. The Evaluation Group's review of the completion report says that in Burundi "compensations were paid in full for 8,265 people for a total amount of Burundian Franc (BIF) 105,311,800 (equivalent of approximately US$67,000 in April 2015)", and that "115 people were yet to be paid compensation at project closure". The documents do not say what the 8,265 people lost, do not break the sum down, and do not say why the 115 were not paid. In Kenya the review says no resettlement was needed. In Madagascar compensation was paid in full, US$56,941 under the resettlement plan and US$9,241 under the environmental and social management plan; the resettlement plan of July 2012 for zones 1A and 2 covers four affected people at four of the 68 sites, with a budget of 43,562,500 ariary, and records that at one site only two households were involved so the survey results did not have to be posted publicly.
burundi-fibre-backbone-unpaid-compensati.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1 for this project. The Evaluation Group's review counts 8,265 people compensated in Burundi and 115 still unpaid at closing; no document opened counts anyone moved.
burundi-fibre-backbone-unpaid-compensati.outcome: The network was working when the project closed. The review records that the authorities revoked the public-private status of Burundi Backbone System and nationalised it in January 2017, "without consultation or compensation", officially on the grounds that the shareholders were not respecting their contractual terms, and rates the sustainability risk Significant for that reason. No document opened says whether the 115 people were ever paid.

companies.name: Uganda Electricity Transmission Company Limited (UETCL)

mutundwe-thermal-plant-land-and-homes.community: The resettlement plan of November 2006 for the Mutundwe thermal plant says the construction "will affect one lady in a negative manner", through the loss of land and crops: one acre of her private mailo land next to the existing Mutundwe substation, and the crops she had grown on it. It counts about 200 people who would be affected indirectly, most of them within 100 metres of the substation, through traffic, dust and noise, and says the survey showed that no homestead would be displaced by the power supply works and that nothing along the 0.2 km access stretch from the Nalukolongo community road would be affected. The completion report tells it differently. It says the mitigation measures included "compensation and resettlement for residents near the plant in other areas for the duration of the PPA", a 5-metre noise barrier to cut the noise, a change to the lighting system, a change to the ignition times to reduce the smell of diesel at start-up, and "monitoring of households that were resettled out of the plant site". Neither the report nor the Evaluation Group's review of it counts those households or says what they were paid. The review adds that the report "does not contain information on the degree of satisfaction of project-affected persons with their compensation and resettlement arrangements".
mutundwe-thermal-plant-land-and-homes.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1 for this project, which matches the one woman whose land and crops the November 2006 resettlement plan says would be affected. The completion report says households were resettled out of the plant site but gives no number, and no document opened counts them.
mutundwe-thermal-plant-land-and-homes.outcome: The plant was commissioned about a year later than planned, after long negotiation of the power purchase agreement over who would carry the fuel supply risk; the completion report gives the commissioning date as July 2008 in one place and says the plant was set in operation in August 2008 in another. By the project's close it was contributing about 15 per cent of Uganda's electricity generation. The report records that in the period after the project some thermal plant operators had to switch off their plants because of accumulated non-payment. Under the same project the government, the Bujagali operator and the Busoga Kingdom signed an agreement to build shrines and pay for ceremonies to move the Bujagali spirits, and the report says the spirits were relocated in early June 2011.

imusho-village-moved-from-national-park.title: Imusho Village Moved Out of Mosi-oa-Tunya National Park
imusho-village-moved-from-national-park.place: Mosi-oa-Tunya National Park, Livingstone, Southern Province, Zambia
imusho-village-moved-from-national-park.point: OpenStreetMap node for Mosi-oa-Tunya National Park. The village stood in the park's western sector on the bank of the Zambezi, and the new site was about 10 km away on the park's western boundary between the Zoological Park and Fariland Farm.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Support for Economic Expansion and Diversification, SEED (P071407, with P074258), Credit IDA-39660 of SDR 19.2 million (US$28.15 million equivalent) and a Global Environment Facility grant TF-53349 of US$4 million, approved 29 July 2004, effective 10 November 2004. The resettlement of Imusho village was carried out before the credit became effective, under a resettlement action plan prepared for this project in September 2003 and cleared by the lender. The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory (29 June 2012).

companies.name: Zambia Wildlife Authority (ZAWA)
companies.role: Approved the move and carried out the resettlement plan; its Technical and Operations Committee took the decision on 14 August 2002
companies.desc: The statutory Zambian body that then managed the country's national parks and game management areas, under the ministry responsible for tourism, environment and natural resources.

imusho-village-moved-from-national-park.community: Imusho village stood inside the fence of Mosi-oa-Tunya National Park, in the park's western sector on the bank of the Zambezi. The Litunga of Barotseland set it up in the 1890s as an immigration control post near the main river crossing. Two families lived there, the Imushos under Village Headman Imusho and the Makumbas, who took the land in the 1890s and whose ancestors are all buried on the site. In November 2001 the village held 35 adult men, 12 adult women and 13 children. They lived on the park's water, fish, fruit and firewood and grew maize and vegetables on about 4 hectares of cleared land, of which about 2 hectares were fenced with three strands of barbed wire; wild animals often destroyed the crops. They drew water from the Zambezi with three pumps and had no services beyond the feeder road to the Livingstone-Mulobezi road. The resettlement plan of September 2003 records that plans to move the village had been running since the late 1980s and that the village had already been moved to different sites inside the park more than three times. The Sakala Land Commission had recommended that the land be cut out of the park as an enclave. After meetings with the park authorities and the office of the deputy minister for Southern Province, the plan says, the village agreed to move to a site of about 233.53 hectares some 10 km away on the park's western boundary, with title to the new land, and the wildlife authority's Technical and Operations Committee approved the move on 14 August 2002. The plan says all the village people would move together to keep the village intact, that compensation for buildings and fruit trees would be paid at replacement cost without depreciation and before anyone moved, that transport and moving expenses would be provided, and that anyone who chose to stay could do so by prior agreement with the authority. It records that an elephant killed a woman within the village site in June 2003, and gives safety from dangerous animals as one of the reasons for moving. The completion report says that, guided by the plan, "resettlement took place prior effectiveness" and "included adequate compensation as determined by a Bank social specialist". Elsewhere the report records that in the Namwala Game Management Area "people were displaced from the GMA conservation zone after an instruction issued by the land chiefs", and that the Bank concluded there was no non-compliance with its safeguards because its resettlement policy "does not apply to restrictions of access to natural resources under community-based projects" as long as appropriate measures to mitigate adverse impacts are identified, which it says was the case at Namwala. A resettlement plan was also carried out at Mukuni Park in Livingstone, and the project's own output table records a partial resettlement of Songwe village for a boundary adjustment.
imusho-village-moved-from-national-park.displaced_note: ICIJ gives no displacement estimate for this project. The resettlement plan of September 2003 counts the village population in November 2001 as 35 adult men, 12 adult women and 13 children. No document opened states a total for the village, and none counts the people actually moved or the people displaced from the Namwala Game Management Area.
imusho-village-moved-from-national-park.killed_note: The September 2003 resettlement plan records that an elephant killed a woman within the village site in June 2003, and gives safety from dangerous animals as a reason for moving the village. That death was not caused by the project.
imusho-village-moved-from-national-park.outcome: The project closed with an outcome rating of Moderately Satisfactory. Mukuni Park was rehabilitated and handed over in 2008 to the Mukuni Management Trust, which collects the park's revenue and rent from the curio sellers. No document opened says what happened to the people of Imusho after the move, how many were moved, or how many people were displaced from the Namwala Game Management Area.

imusho-village-moved-from-national-park.confidence_note: The village's history, population and the terms of the move come from the borrower's own resettlement plan, published by the World Bank, and describe what was planned. The completion report confirms in one sentence that the move happened before the credit became effective and that compensation was judged adequate by a Bank social specialist; it gives no count, no date and no amount, and no monitoring report on the village was found. p075997-cape-biodiversity-coleske.drop_reason: No one was moved and the loss of work that the people suffered came from a land purchase the project did not finance. The ICIJ figure of 35 is the 35 households of former farm workers at Coleske, inside the core zone of the Baviaanskloof Mega-Reserve, whose resettlement the project planned for and never carried out. The completion report (25 April 2011, para 37-39) says the proposed resettlement of the Coleske farm workers "was not completed by project close", that "a segment of the Coleske community has continued to decline ECBP's resettlement offers", that without their agreement the Eastern Cape Parks Board "has not yet moved forward with the option of seeking a court order that would require the resettlement to take place", and that the project "did not include funding for any such resettlement", which would be paid for with government money if it ever happened. The same paragraphs record that Coleske Farm was bought by the Eastern Cape department in 2001, "well before the start of the BCSD project", between willing buyer and willing seller, that no provision was made for the farm's agricultural workers and that none of them hold land ownership rights under South African law. On the outcome for those people the report says the final Bank mission visited the site, met many of the residents and concluded that the project had adequately addressed their livelihood concerns, that the parks board agreed specific uses of natural resources inside the reserve and gave Coleske residents preference for work including 10 staff jobs, and that the residents "have thus been able to maintain or improve their livelihoods" while waiting for the government's decision. The Evaluation Group's review repeats all of this. Checked against the outcome documents: the completion report's own safeguards section says that for the rest of the project the resettlement and process frameworks were not needed because protected area expansion came from re-assigned state forestry land and voluntary stewardship agreements, and that marine zoning followed the process framework, giving Betty's Bay as an example agreed with local stakeholders. Two outside documents by the same author point the other way and are recorded here so the row can be reopened: a April 2009 paper by Eleanor Macgregor of the Wilderness Foundation, published on the implementing agency's website, says eight people had held permanent jobs on the farm with more than 100 dependents between them, that temporary work was arranged for 40 people when the farm was bought, that residents had used the land for grazing donkeys, acacia wood, medicinal plants and honey, that the department was legally bound only to offer equivalent housing in the nearest town about 100 km away, and that Willowmore and Steytlerville have extremely high unemployment; and the same author's 2014 master's dissertation at the University of the Free State finds that "the general situation of Coleske has deteriorated" since the land was bought. Both describe harm that begins with the 2001 purchase, which this GEF grant did not finance, and neither records anyone being moved.

p126579-eastern-electricity-highway.note: Confirmed by place and years as well as by P-number: the existing case covers the Kenya side of the Eastern Electricity Highway from Laikipia to Suswa, 2017 to 2024, and already carries the 2,638 affected people, the 832 still owed land compensation at closing in January 2024, the 96 and 13 still owed for crops and structures in April 2024, the two fatal accidents, the 200 families who lost communal grazing land and the livestock feed plant. The documents harvested for this round add no fact that is not already in the existing case. The 2016 resettlement plan on disk gives plan figures only: 345 people in 52 households losing farmland and trees at the ground electrode site, and around 200 households, about 1,000 people, counted as using the communal grazing area.
